A 1RM test at the end of Phase 3 (end of Week 12) can be a useful, objective measure of maximal strength progress — but given this client’s PCOS, history of irregular cycles, recent higher‑intensity training and the risk of under‑recovery from her aggressive plan, it must be implemented cautiously. Below I’ll cover benefits, risks, when to do it, safe protocols you can use instead of a true 1RM, step‑by‑step procedures if you decide to test, and safety/monitoring rules.

Quick recommendation
- Do a submaximal 1RM estimation or a properly supervised testing session (not an all‑out, unsupervised 1RM grind). Prefer a 3–5RM or an RPE‑based heavy single at ~RPE 8.5 as the primary test. Only attempt a true 1RM if: the client is well recovered (good sleep, steady energy, no menstrual worsening), you have a spotter and coach present, and medical team aware if needed.
- If you want a single objective metric with lower risk, run a 3RM or 5RM test (predict 1RM from those lifts) or use an RPE 9 top set protocol. These are safer and still very useful for programming.

Why test (benefits)
- Objective measure of strength progress and training effectiveness.
- Motivation: a measurable outcome can boost adherence.
- Helps set percentages for next training block if using %1RM programming.

Risks (especially relevant to this client)
- Maximal attempts raise injury risk without perfect technique and warm‑up.
- Heavy maximal lifting increases acute physiological stress (neural, hormonal) which could impair recovery and potentially affect menstrual/hormonal balance in a susceptible client.
- If client is in an aggressive calorie deficit or performing frequent HIIT, recovery may be inadequate to safely perform true 1RMs.

When to test (timing and prerequisites)
- Only test at the end of Week 12 if:
  - Client reports consistent good recovery over the prior 2 weeks (sleep ≥7–8 h, energy high, no increased soreness, resistance performance intact).
  - No worsening menstrual symptoms for the prior month.
  - Trainer and spotter are available to supervise all maximal attempts.
  - Client has a solid technical base on the lifts to be tested.
  - Preferably schedule test at least 48–72 hours after the last heavy HIIT/resistance session (to avoid residual fatigue).
- If any red flags, choose submaximal testing instead.

Safer alternatives to true 1RM (recommended)
- 3RM or 5RM test on major lifts (squat, bench, deadlift). Use validated equations to estimate 1RM.
  - Pros: lower rep max is taxing but safer; still strongly predictive of 1RM.
- Top single at RPE 8.5 (heavy but shy of true maximal) — repeatable and lower stress.
- Velocity or RPE‑based testing if you have access to a linear position transducer or reliable RPE scoring.
- Isometric mid‑thigh pull (if equipment available) gives objective measure with lower injury risk.

If you proceed with a true 1RM test — step‑by‑step protocol (safe, conservative)
1) Pre‑test screening
  - Confirm wellness scores for the previous 7–14 days (sleep, energy, soreness, mood all acceptable).
  - Confirm no recent (last 2 weeks) illness, injury, or menstrual disturbance.
  - Ensure client has had adequate nutrition in the 24–48 hours prior (no aggressive caloric restriction on test day).
  - Get consent from client and note that a spotter will be present.

2) Scheduling
  - Test in the morning or early afternoon (not late evening).
  - Avoid same day as HIIT or long cardio. Schedule at least 48–72 hours after last heavy session.

3) Warm up (20–30 minutes total)
  - 5–8 min general cardio (light bike/walk).
  - Joint mobility and movement prep for the lift.
  - Specific ramp sets (example for squat):
    - Empty bar x 8–10
    - 40% estimated 1RM x 5
    - 60% x 3
    - 70% x 2
    - 80% x 1 (rest 2–4 min)
    - 90% x 1 (rest 3–5 min) — if it feels good, proceed
  - Use RPE to judge readiness; if any ramp set feels unusually heavy, stop.

4) Testing protocol (conservative)
  - After warm up, attempt a projected 1RM single at RPE 9 (very hard but not absolute max). Rest 3–5 min between attempts.
  - If successful and client feels good, increase weight by 2.5–5% and attempt another single (max 2–3 heavy attempts total).
  - Stop testing if client reports sharp pain, dizziness, nausea, or if movement breakdown appears.
  - Use spotters and safety bars (especially for squat/bench) and perform deadlifts from blocks or with trap bar if concerned about low‑back stress.
  - Keep total number of heavy singles low (3 attempts per lift max recommended).

5) Post‑test recovery
  - Cool down, mobility, and light aerobic work.
  - Consume a larger post‑test meal: 30–40 g protein + 60–80 g carbs to aid recovery and replenish glycogen.
  - Avoid heavy sessions for 48–72 hours post test (light mobility or LISS only).

Specifics per lift (practical choices)
- Squat: use safety pins or a spotter; consider using a box squat for testing if technique or mobility limits exist.
- Bench press: always use competent spotters.
- Deadlift: consider trap bar or 3RM instead of an absolute 1RM. Trap bar 1RM is often safer for many clients.
- If technique on any lift is inconsistent under submaximal loads, do not test that lift to 1RM.

Documentation and follow‑up
- Record warm‑up loads, attempts, RPE and video (if possible) for form review.
- Use 3–5RM estimated 1RM if true 1RM wasn’t attempted.
- Review results with the client and plan the next block based on both absolute and relative progress (strength per bodyweight, symmetry, wellness).

Decision flowchart (simple)
- Wellness, sleep, energy + cycle stable for 2 wks → proceed with submaximal 3–5RM or RPE 8.5 top single.
- If all of the above plus coach/spotter present + client wants max test → consider true 1RM with conservative protocol and strict stopping rules.
- If any recovery or menstrual red flags → postpone testing and retest after 4 weeks of recovery/adjusted training/nutrition.

Bottom line
- I support testing strength at the end of Phase 3, but prefer a submaximal 3–5RM or RPE‑based heavy single for safety and to protect hormonal and recovery status. If you want a full 1RM test, only do it under strict supervision, with proper warm up, fueling, and stopping rules.
